<reason>Side A won a solid victory through superior causal depth and a textbook strategic trap across the second half of the debate. Side A established specific physiological and economic mechanisms early on—most notably how brief jail stints destroy physical tolerance and trigger fatal post-release overdoses, how fear of arrest deters witnesses from calling 911, and how criminal records lock recovering addicts out of legal employment. Side B mounted a plausible counter-case centered on coerced treatment leverage and aggregate user scale, but caught itself in a fatal contradiction: insisting that treatment uptake collapses without a "criminal penalty" while simultaneously denying that enforcement cycles relapsing addicts through jail. Side A pinned this contradiction down in Pressure Questions and capitalized decisively in Closing when Side B redefined its "coercive backstop" as outpatient care, residential treatment, and medical detention—tools that are civil and medical rather than criminal. Side A also answered Side B's crime questions directly (such as showing how medication-assisted treatment like methadone removes the daily financial compulsion to steal), whereas Side B grew repetitive and included nonexistent reference IDs ([C2.2, C2.4]) in its second rebuttal.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Q1 [A3.1] and Closing [A5.1-A5.3]: Side A forced Side B to specify what the "coercive backstop" of punitive enforcement actually is when an addict relapses, if not a tolerance-destroying jail stint. When Side B answered in [B4.1] that the backstop is graduated clinical care and "medical detention" rather than jail, Side A pointed out that Side B had stripped out everything criminal (jail and convictions) and conceded Side A's public health model.</best_rebuttal>
